en: Your mother's heart was terribly troubled.
Carrying two people side by side,
Your mother went like a racer.
None could match her steps;
No soul could match her pace.
Your mother walked without tiring;
Your sister-in-law nearly grew exhausted.
Your mother bent and shrank with pain.
The dark blood flowing from her side
Streamed down along her soft boots.
Her spine ached sharply;
The flesh of her soles tore apart.
Her soles were beaten on the stones,
Her forehead scorched by the blazing sun.
The wide world narrowed down;
She could not make it across Keng-Kol.
For your mother, the wide world narrowed;
Your mother could not cross Chapchyk's pass,
Your mother, weary and worn, could not walk.
She could not cross Küyük Pass;
Your mother, burning with grief, could not walk.
She could not cross Zhorgo Pass;
Your mother, weeping in sorrow, could not walk.
Across plains where even owls did not fly,
Walking alone and wearing herself out,
Your sister-in-law suffered hardship,
Meeting with such a fate.
In the lowlands where foxes did not roam,
Walking by night, distressed—
Ah, ruined world, may you never prosper!
She met with such affliction.
Across dark ridges where shelducks did not fly,
She flew onward through the wilds without turning back.
How much anguish your mother endured,
For the child born from her womb!
All her thoughts were torn apart.
When she reached the yellow hills,
Blood spurted from her calves,
Pouring down over her heels.
When Kanykei tried to walk,
Dark blood flowed from her calves.
Her soles burned and wore hollow.
From the burden of carrying your mother,
The flesh of her soles was stripped away.
When she stepped, the flesh of her soles tore apart.
Even when your mother lay still,
She cried out in fear of the villains.
What she grasped became embers;
What she waded through became ankle-deep blazing fire.
The wide world narrowed down;
She yearned, unable to reach Bukhara.
Without outer shoes, wearing stockings,
The wretched soul suffered grief.
Without boots, wearing stockings,
The wretched soul would not die.
Oluya-Ata and Chong-Merki—
She crossed the land between them.
To the rugged hills
Your mother came, weeping bitterly.
On Kazy-Kurt's sloping ground,
Your dear mother found support,
Then toward the dark plain beyond,
Your mother reached it, bent low.
If you looked in certain places,
There were low, rounded ridges.
Looming through the haze,
It was a desert no human trod.
Not a mountain even ankle-sized—
It was a place to cast one into hell.
For Kanykei, suffering torment,
The time to meet it had arrived.
Its saxaul and green thorns
Pierced her soles with stabbing pain.
The red sands of the plain
Rustled inside her boots.
Offering supplication to God,
Your mother wandered toward Bukhara, sobbing.
Then Kanykei went in mourning;
Semetey went in flight.
Kanykei went as a widow;
Semetey went as a wanderer.
In Chyiyrdy's old age,
Making her ride upon another's back,
This treacherous world brought grief.
Kanykei, who rode no ambling horse,
It put on the road and made to suffer.
The wide world narrowed down;
Unable to reach Bukhara, she was abased.
Seeing your sister-in-law's condition,
If she had come to such a state,
Who might not come to the same?
As your sister-in-law went weeping,
The birch wept, the willow wept.
Looking at your sister-in-law,
Every living creature wept.
Of the dark plain below,
She reached the ledge.
The eye could not encompass it;
Words could not exhaust its telling.
A shelduck flying there would weaken;
If a little bustard took wing across it,
Its wingtips would grow weary.
A black vulture would fly until stiff,
Its palate dry, and lie motionless.
No furrow had been touched by a plow;
No burrow had been dug by a marmot.
There was no grass stem to stumble on,
No stone to crack a marrowbone,
No pit, no hollow, no wild beast.
Carrying them both together,
Traveling across the open wilds,
Kanykei had no good fortune.
When she stood worn and weary,
To come out and meet her
There was no swift Taibuurul either.
Shrunken like a gnawed-clean head,
Your mother Kanykei had no good fortune.
Weary in that vast wilderness,
She had no swift horse to catch and ride.
Someone who would grieve to see her—
Of those dear Kyrgyz people,
She had no kinsman for a companion.
The wide world narrowed down.
Carrying them both together,
That distant Bukhara—
She longed to see it just once.
How could your mother spare herself?
For seven days she traveled without rest,
Valuing her wretched life less than a hair.
Hurting the flesh of her calves,
Rubbing her heels raw,
Seven days and nights,
Without sleeping propped on an elbow,
Without taking a peaceful nap,
Without turning her eyes to sleep,
Without setting her hip upon the earth,
Seven days and nights—
How did your mother spare herself?
To the banks of a flowing river
Your mother came,
To the banks of the Syr Darya.
There lay the Syr Darya,
Words could not exhaust its telling,
The eye could not reach its farther shore.
If you looked at that time,
The Syr Darya's waters had risen.
A flood ran over them;
The glacier heads were pouring down,
Clear streams joined from its flanks.
It had risen beyond measure.
Smelling of clay and turned to mud,
It had swollen ceaselessly.
The flooding waters overflowed;
They rose above the willow tops.
Foam glittered on the surface,
The water murmured in the depths—
So high had it risen.
The flesh of her soles beaten raw,
Trapped on reaching the Syr Darya,
Your mother stood crying out.
Too many sorrows to fit within her breast,
Your royal sister-in-law Kanykei,
Her tears flowed ten ways.
'My deep-dug pit of sorrow—
Making even the water my enemy,
O God, whom I beseech,
You mean to show me quite a marvel!
If, instead, wretched me,
I step down into the river,
The orphan in my arms—
Will it cruelly treat him?
My mother on my back—
Will its flood come and tear her away?
Battering me against the stones,
My mountainlike body—
Will it turn it mottled red?
All my arms and legs—
Will it cruelly tear them off?
Parted from my blood-shedding hero,
I have become a fleeing woman.
Not letting me take a single step,
You have become the river barring my way.
Kozhakmat, to whom I pledged my hand,
When will you turn your eyes upon me?
Forty chiltens, with whom I joined hands,
O God, when will you lend support?
My perfected patrons, vast as rivers,
This bitch without a share of blessing—
When will you lend her support?
Black-spotted leopard,
Companion of my blood-shedding hero,
Charge forth beside me!
Short-tailed lion,
Patrons who supported my blood-shedding hero,
Come to me this very day!
Forty chiltens, my Khizyr Iliyas,
I am hard-pressed; give me passage today!
Barefoot red dervish,
Give me your hand, do not leave me grieving.
Great river flowing with a roar,
Give a grieving soul passage today!'
Sobbing in supplication,
Your swift-steed mother Kanykei
Collapsed where she stood, crying out.
Your widowed mother Kanykei
Stood weeping bitterly.
Worn out by weeping,
Your mother made her prayer,
Beseeching the forty chiltens:
'I have suffered straits, O world.
Will he reach spacious Bukhara?
For seven days he has gone hungry,
This Semetey here—
O God, will he die today?
Mother, whom I cherish,
Shall I dwell along the cliffs?
"Her only child and her mother—
Kanykei, suffering hardship,
Killed them in her despair
And was left alone," they might say.
Shall I earn such an evil name?
For seven days your child has tasted nothing;
He may die of hunger.
Mother, whom I cherish,
Perhaps his death will come like this.
For me, a bereaved wretch,
Perhaps all hope will fail like this!
The dear hair growing on my head,
Mother, let me divide and braid in four.
For the only child my lord left behind,
Mother, let me die in sacrifice.
Remaining alive in such distress,
Mother, whom I cherish,
What desire could I fulfill?
For the little one my khan left behind,
Rather than this, let me give myself in sacrifice.
Mother, give me Ak Tinte; let me take it,
Let me thrust it into my lung like this.
Rather than remain alive this way,
Mother, whom I cherish,
Let me die in sacrifice for you both.'
On the banks of the Syr Darya,
Where your mother was trapped,
Kanykei made her lodging.
Camped, weeping, resting there—
Let me leave her thus,
And the leopard Bakai, the mighty sultan,
Let me begin with your uncle.
Your fierce-wolf uncle Bakai's
Battle cry was like the call to prayer.
Placed in front, he brought good fortune;
His towering back was like countless armies.
He was the son of a holy elder;
He was a servant beloved of God.
He found a way in darkness,
Found the right words in an unforeseen plight.
